scripts.opening:opening:
[measured] Women of Prairie Avenue.

[short pause] A spring morning, 1904. The men of this street have gone downtown to their stores, banks and packing houses, and their names are on everything. [short pause] Their wives, sisters and daughters are not allowed to vote for president, and won't be for another nine years.

[short pause] They are busy anyway. [short pause] Six houses on foot, 1608 to 2115 Prairie, north to south, and at each a woman the sources tie to the house: a nurse's champion, a future detective, a diarist with a silversmith's bench in her basement, a suffragist, a fountain-builder and the street's last great lady.

[short pause] Begin at the north end, with two sisters who walked into a club that had never let anyone like them in.
scripts.stop:frank: [measured] 1608 Prairie, the Frank household. [short pause] Henrietta Greenebaum Frank worked year after year for better nursing education at the Illinois Training School for Nurses. In 1876 she and her sister Hannah Greenebaum Solomon became the first Jewish members of the prestigious Chicago Woman's Club. [short pause] Hannah went on to found the National Council of Jewish Women and was its first president. Two sisters, one door opened. [short pause] A block south, a young mother is living in a house her parents built for her.
scripts.stop:lee: [measured] 1700 Prairie, built by John and Frances Glessner for their daughter, Frances, who married Blewett Lee in 1898. [short pause] Right now she is a society wife. Wait. Decades from now she will build eighteen tiny, perfect rooms, each one a death scene in miniature for students to solve: the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death, still used to train investigators. [short pause] She will help found Harvard's Department of Legal Medicine, and in 1943 she will become the first woman police captain in the United States. [short pause] Her mother lives one block south, and is probably writing about her right now.
scripts.stop:glessner: [measured] 1800 Prairie, Glessner House. [short pause] Frances Macbeth Glessner began a journal in 1879 and kept it for forty years, and the house museum still writes the family's story from it. She kept bees. [short pause] Since 1893 her Monday Morning Reading Class has met in the library, women reading together every week through the winter and spring. [short pause] And this year, 1904, she has set up a silversmith's workbench in the basement and begun making silver with her own hands. [short pause] Across Eighteenth Street and down the west walk, a neighbour is fighting for something bigger.
scripts.stop:jones: [measured] 1834 Prairie, the Fernando Jones house. [short pause] Jane Grahame Jones was, in the words of the city's encyclopedia, a longtime and outspoken activist for woman suffrage; her husband's scrapbook keeps clippings on the Illinois Woman Suffrage Association from as early as 1875. [short pause] She has been at it for nearly thirty years and still cannot vote. In 1913 Illinois will become the first state east of the Mississippi to let women vote for president. The house is razed in 1942. [short pause] Keep walking south, past Twentieth Street, to a family that will give the city a fountain.
scripts.stop:buckingham: [measured] 2036 Prairie, the Buckingham house, where the 1904 Blue Book lists Clarence Buckingham, philanthropist and businessman. [short pause] His sister was Kate Sturges Buckingham, philanthropist and art patron. [short pause] In 1927, after his death, she will give Chicago the Buckingham Fountain in his memory: twice the size of the Versailles fountain it copies, with a centre jet that throws water 150 feet into the air. [short pause] One more house, and the woman who stayed after everyone else had gone.
scripts.stop:armour: [measured] 2115 Prairie, the Kelley-Armour house. [short pause] The 1904 Blue Book lists Mrs. Philip D. Armour here; the census of 1900 names her Belle, born in Ohio. Her husband, the meatpacker, died in 1901. [short pause] As the great families died or moved away to suburbs like Lake Forest, she stayed on, and on. [short pause] The district marker says Armour's widow was among the last residents of the street, dying here in 1927, long after most of her neighbours' houses had been sold or torn down. [short pause] Hers follows in 1937.
scripts.ending:finish:
[measured] End of the walk at 2115 Prairie. Six women, six houses. [short pause] A nurse's champion, a detective, a diarist, a suffragist, a fountain-builder and a widow who would not leave.

[short pause] They are only the ones the sources name. Behind every one of these fronts lived maids, cooks, nurses and laundresses whose names are only in the census. [short pause] Their stories are waiting too.
